records.evidenceSource: Stripe pricing page (percentage + fixed fee per successful card charge, e.g. 2.9% + $0.30 in the US).
records.assignmentRationale: Revenue is earned per payment processed—a classic transaction-based model documented directly on the public pricing page.

records.evidenceSource: Stripe API reference documentation; integration guides for developers; absence of end-consumer-facing application UI as the core product.
records.assignmentRationale: The product is delivered primarily through APIs and developer integrations rather than a standalone end-user application—among the most canonical API-based delivery cases in software.

records.evidenceSource: Stripe.com positioning toward businesses and developers accepting payments; no direct offering to end consumers as customers.
records.assignmentRationale: Stripe sells exclusively to merchants, platforms, and developers who need payment acceptance—not to the paying consumer.

records.evidenceSource: Stripe Connect documentation; marketplace and platform payment flows connecting merchants and payers.
records.assignmentRationale: Stripe structurally connects merchants/businesses that collect payments with consumers who pay—two distinct sides with different incentives and platform rules.

records.evidenceSource: Stripe developer documentation, test-mode onboarding, and widespread bottom-up integration by individual developers before organizational rollout.
records.assignmentRationale: Adoption typically begins with a developer integrating the API in a project, then expanding to production and organizational commitment—classic dev-tool PLG.

records.evidenceSource: Stripe company history; partner/integration ecosystem (plugins, platforms); displacement of legacy payment gateways and bank-centric intermediaries.
records.assignmentRationale: Stripe entered the market by disrupting traditional payment intermediaries through a partner-rich integration ecosystem, redefining how software businesses embed payments.
